title: Why Giving A “Look” Is A Poor Classroom Management Strategy agement-strategy/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques the common strategy of giving misbehaving students a stern, silent 'look' to curb disruption, arguing that despite its short-term effectiveness, it causes long-term harm. He identifies the practice as antagonistic, since it creates a personal, adversarial dynamic and communicates dislike rather than impersonal accountability. It's also confusing, he notes, because students often can't be sure what behavior triggered the look or even whether it was directed at them, undermining the clarity effective classroom management requires. Finally, it's inconsistent, breaking a teacher's promise to follow a stated classroom management plan and instead substituting intimidation. Linsin argues that even though 'the look' may stop a specific instance of misbehavior, it damages the underlying relationship and a teacher's long-term influence, making students less motivated academically and more likely to misbehave when unobserved.
points: Giving students a silent 'look' to curb misbehavior may work momentarily but damages long-term teacher-student relationships.
The strategy is antagonistic, creating a personal, us-against-them dynamic rather than impersonal accountability.
It's also confusing, since students often can't be certain what behavior triggered the look or that it was even meant for them.
Using intimidation instead of a stated classroom management plan is a form of inconsistency that undermines trust.
Avoiding intimidation-based strategies preserves a teacher's likability, influence, and ability to teach without friction.
quotes: Whenever you glare at students, or otherwise try to intimidate them into behaving, you create a you-against-them relationship.

You make it personal. You give the impression that not only are you angry, but you dislike them personally. After all, when someone gives a dirty look, that’s the natural conclusion—especially with children.
When you give a “look,” you have no way of knowing whether your students understand what it means. They may not even be sure you’re looking at them or what behavior you’re referring to.
When you promise to follow your classroom management plan, but then go back on your word and glare instead, you send the message that you can’t be trusted.
But now Robert can’t stand his teacher and has little motivation to push himself academically.
You must follow your classroom management plan as its written and give them an opportunity to take responsibility all on their own—without your dirty looks, lectures, or two cents.
